title: Newton's Inequality, First Rung (n = 3): S₂² ≥ S₁S₃
description: Resolves the concrete case n = 3 of the open question 'prove the next Maclaurin/Newton rung S₂² ≥ S₁S₃', the log-concavity of the elementary symmetric means and the first rung that requires genuinely more than Cauchy-Schwarz. For reals a,b,c with e₁ = a+b+c, e₂ = ab+bc+ca, e₃ = abc, the symmetric means S₁ = e₁/3, S₂ = e₂/3, S₃ = e₃ satisfy S₂² ≥ S₁S₃, equivalently the cleared form e₂² ≥ 3·e₁·e₃. The engine is an explicit sum-of-squares certificate e₂² − 3e₁e₃ = ½[(ab−bc)² + (bc−ca)² + (ca−ab)²], a pure ring identity, giving the inequality for ALL reals (no nonnegativity, unlike Maclaurin), together with the equality characterization ab = bc = ca. 5 theorems, 3 definitions, 0 axioms.

overview.historicalContext: Isaac Newton observed that the elementary symmetric means S_k = e_k / C(n,k) of n real numbers are log-concave: S_k² ≥ S_{k-1}·S_{k+1} for 1 ≤ k ≤ n−1. These Newton inequalities refine and interpolate the Maclaurin chain S₁ ≥ √S₂ ≥ ∛S₃ ≥ ⋯, whose two ends recover AM ≥ GM. Unlike Maclaurin's inequalities, Newton's inequalities hold for ALL real tuples (not only nonnegative ones), because their classical proof runs through Rolle's theorem: the derivative of a real-rooted polynomial is again real-rooted, and iterating down to a quadratic reduces log-concavity to the nonnegativity of a discriminant. The parent entry (amgm-inequality-oq-02-oq-01-oq-05) formalized the base rung S₁² ≥ S₂, which collapses to Cauchy-Schwarz; its open-questions list asks for the next rung S₂² ≥ S₁S₃, the first that is genuinely stronger. This entry answers it for n = 3 by an elementary sum-of-squares certificate, sidestepping the Rolle machinery.
overview.problemStatement: For reals $a,b,c$ let $e_1 = a+b+c$, $e_2 = ab+bc+ca$, $e_3 = abc$, and the symmetric means $S_1 = e_1/3$, $S_2 = e_2/3$, $S_3 = e_3$. Then $S_2^2 \ge S_1 S_3$, equivalently the cleared form $e_2^2 \ge 3\,e_1 e_3$.
overview.text: The proof rests on a single algebraic identity: the Newton defect equals half a sum of three squares, e₂² − 3e₁e₃ = ½[(ab−bc)² + (bc−ca)² + (ca−ab)²]. Nonnegativity of the right-hand side (three squares) immediately gives the cleared inequality e₂² ≥ 3e₁e₃ for all reals. The averaged form S₂² ≥ S₁S₃ follows by dividing through by the positive constant 9 (the denominators C(3,k) are constants, so no positivity hypotheses on a,b,c are needed). The SOS certificate also reads off the equality case: equality holds iff all three pairwise products ab, bc, ca are equal.
overview.proofStrategy: Three moves. (1) newton_sos_identity: expand e₂² − 3e₁e₃ and match it term-by-term to ½[(ab−bc)² + (bc−ca)² + (ca−ab)²] — a pure `ring` identity after unfolding the definitions. (2) newton_cleared: since the right-hand side of the identity is a sum of squares, `nlinarith` with the three `sq_nonneg` hints (and the identity) closes e₂² ≥ 3e₁e₃. (3) newton_base_step: the averaged defect (e₂/3)² − (e₁/3)·(e₃/1) equals (e₂² − 3e₁e₃)/9 by `ring`, and the numerator is ≥ 0 by step (2), so `div_nonneg` + `linarith` finish. The equality direction newton_eq_of_all_eq (a=b=c ⇒ equality) is a direct `ring` computation; the converse newton_products_eq_of_eq extracts ab=bc=ca from the vanishing sum of squares via `pow_eq_zero_iff`.
keyInsights: At n = 3, Newton's inequality is literally a three-term sum of squares. The defect e₂² − 3e₁e₃ equals ½[(ab−bc)² + (bc−ca)² + (ca−ab)²], so the inequality is an SOS certificate — no Rolle's theorem, no discriminants, no real-rootedness argument is needed at this size.

This rung is strictly beyond Cauchy-Schwarz. The base rung S₁² ≥ S₂ reduces to the power-mean bound n·p₂ ≥ e₁² (Cauchy-Schwarz). The k = 2 rung has no such reduction; its content is the genuinely new SOS above, which is why the parent's open-question flagged it as the first rung requiring more than Cauchy-Schwarz.

No nonnegativity is required. Although Maclaurin's chain assumes nonnegative reals, S₂² ≥ S₁S₃ holds for all real a,b,c because the SOS certificate is sign-agnostic. The nonnegativity hypothesis only becomes essential at Maclaurin rungs where one extracts real roots (√S₂, ∛S₃, …).

The equality locus is exactly ab = bc = ca. Because the defect is a sum of squares of the pairwise differences of the products, equality forces those products to coincide — recovering a = b = c for nonzero variables, the expected extremal configuration.

The general n statement is documented but not proved here: cleared of binomial denominators, Newton's k = 2 inequality reads 2(n−2)·e₂² ≥ 3(n−1)·e₁e₃, reducing to e₂² ≥ 3e₁e₃ at n = 3. Its general proof needs the Rolle/derivative reduction; formalizing that is the forward open question.
prerequisites: Elementary symmetric polynomials e₁, e₂, e₃ of three reals

conclusion.implications: Answers the parent entry's open question 'prove the next Maclaurin rung S₂² ≥ S₁S₃' in the concrete case n = 3, and makes explicit that at this rung the content is a single sum of squares — the first place in the Maclaurin/Newton chain where new inequality content (beyond Cauchy-Schwarz) enters. The SOS identity newton_sos_identity is reusable as a standalone algebraic fact, and the cleared lemma newton_cleared is an integer-polynomial inequality independent of the averaging. The remaining gap is the general-n rung 2(n−2)e₂² ≥ 3(n−1)e₁e₃, whose classical proof goes through Rolle's theorem.
openQuestions: Prove the general-n k = 2 Newton inequality 2(n−2)·e₂² ≥ 3(n−1)·e₁e₃ for all reals (n ≥ 3), via the Rolle/derivative reduction: derivatives of a real-rooted polynomial are real-rooted, reducing to a quadratic discriminant. This requires formalizing that ∏(x − xᵢ)' is real-rooted.
Prove the full Newton chain S_k² ≥ S_{k-1}S_{k+1} for all 1 ≤ k ≤ n−1 and all reals, obtaining Maclaurin's inequality for nonnegative reals as a corollary by chaining the log-concavity bounds.
Formalize the higher n = 4 concrete rungs (S₂² ≥ S₁S₃ and S₃² ≥ S₂S₄) via explicit SOS certificates, testing how far the elementary SOS approach reaches before Rolle's theorem becomes unavoidable.
